items.stem: Which novel is often described as a founding work of Gothic fiction?
items.answer: The Castle of Otranto (Horace Walpole, 1764)
items.markingKey: The Castle of Otranto (Horace Walpole, 1764). Walpole's novel established many Gothic conventions.

items.stem:
Read the following opening of "The Tell-Tale Heart" (1843) by Edgar Allan Poe.

"True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad? The disease had sharpened my senses—not destroyed—not dulled them. Above all was the sense of hearing acute. I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in hell. How, then, am I mad? Hearken! and observe how healthily—how calmly I can tell you the whole story."

Identify three Gothic conventions in this extract and explain how each creates fear.
items.answer: Gothic features: a disturbed mind, a confession, references to hell and the supernatural, and an intense, claustrophobic first-person voice.
items.markingKey: Gothic features: a disturbed mind, a confession, references to hell and the supernatural, and an intense, claustrophobic first-person voice. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following opening of a Gothic short story.

Blackwater Hall had been empty for forty years, yet every night a candle burned in the highest window.
I arrived in November, when the trees had given up their leaves and the fog lay on the moor like a shroud. The gates groaned open before I touched them.
Inside, the air was colder than the night. Portraits lined the staircase – generations of pale Blackwaters – and every pair of painted eyes was turned, I swear, towards the door.
Towards me.

Explain how the writer makes something familiar seem strange or threatening.
items.answer: The familiar becomes strange: painted portraits seem to look at the narrator and gates open without being touched – ordinary objects behave impossibly.
items.markingKey: The familiar becomes strange: painted portraits seem to look at the narrator and gates open without being touched – ordinary objects behave impossibly. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: List four Gothic conventions you could include in a story set in an old lighthouse.
items.answer: Any four: isolation; a storm (pathetic fallacy); a mysterious light or sound; a secret from the past; a ghost or uncanny object; a frightened first-person narrator.
items.markingKey: Any four: isolation; a storm (pathetic fallacy); a mysterious light or sound; a secret from the past; a ghost or uncanny object; a frightened first-person narrator.

items.stem: Distinguish between pace and tension.
items.answer: Pace is how fast the story seems to move; tension is the anxious feeling in the reader. Slowing the pace at a key moment can increase tension.

items.stem:
Read the following opening of "The Tell-Tale Heart" (1843) by Edgar Allan Poe.

"True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad? The disease had sharpened my senses—not destroyed—not dulled them. Above all was the sense of hearing acute. I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in hell. How, then, am I mad? Hearken! and observe how healthily—how calmly I can tell you the whole story."

How does Poe present the narrator as unreliable in this opening? Focus on sentence structure and pacing.
items.answer: The narrator protests his sanity too strongly: the opening "True!—nervous" and the repeated "very, very dreadfully" use dashes and repetition that mimic agitation. His rhetorical questions ("How, then, am I mad?") try to persuade the reader but reveal desperation, and the hyperbolic claim to hear "things in hell" exposes distorted perception. The direct address "Hearken!" makes us his audience, yet the contrast between his claim of calm and his frantic syntax teaches us not to trust him.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The narrator protests his sanity too strongly: the opening "True!—nervous" and the repeated "very, very dreadfully" use dashes and repetition that mimic agitation. His rhetorical questions ("How, then, am I mad?") try to persuade the reader but reveal desperation, and the hyperbolic claim to hear "things in hell" exposes distorted perception. The direct address "Hearken!" makes us his audience, yet the contrast between his claim of calm and his frantic syntax teaches us not to trust him. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: "Sentence structure creates more tension than vocabulary." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Sentence structure and vocabulary work together, but structure is often what turns frightening words into a heart-stopping moment.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rhythm controls pace and shock; fragments and white space create pauses. Arguments against: vivid, threatening words create fear; tension comes from both together. Supported judgement: Sentence structure and vocabulary work together, but structure is often what turns frightening words into a heart-stopping moment. items.stem:
Read the following extract from a Gothic short story told by a teenage narrator.

My brother says I imagine things. He's probably right. I imagined the scratching behind the wallpaper. I imagined that the mirror in the hall shows the room as it was a hundred years ago – the gas lamps, the dark curtains, the woman in grey.
Last night I imagined she turned round.
This morning there were wet footprints on the stairs. Small ones. Bare.
My brother says I must have walked in my sleep. I didn't tell him that my feet were dry.

To what extent should the reader trust this narrator? Refer to the text.
items.answer: The narrator undermines herself by repeating "I imagined", which makes us doubt her; but the physical evidence (wet footprints, her dry feet) contradicts the brother's rational explanation.
items.markingKey: The narrator undermines herself by repeating "I imagined", which makes us doubt her; but the physical evidence (wet footprints, her dry feet) contradicts the brother's rational explanation. items.stem:
Read the following opening of "The Tell-Tale Heart" (1843) by Edgar Allan Poe.

"True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad? The disease had sharpened my senses—not destroyed—not dulled them. Above all was the sense of hearing acute. I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in hell. How, then, am I mad? Hearken! and observe how healthily—how calmly I can tell you the whole story."

Analyse how the writer uses sentence structure in "Hearken! and observe" to create tension.
items.answer: Direct address: "Hearken! and observe" – the narrator speaks directly to "you", making the reader a listener to a confession.
items.markingKey: Direct address: "Hearken! and observe" – the narrator speaks directly to "you", making the reader a listener to a confession. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the uncanny is more disturbing than an obvious monster.
items.answer: When familiar things become strange, readers feel that even safe, everyday spaces are not to be trusted, which unsettles them deeply.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When familiar things become strange, readers feel that even safe, everyday spaces are not to be trusted, which unsettles them deeply. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a reliable narrator and an unreliable narrator.
items.answer: A reliable narrator gives an account the reader can trust; an unreliable narrator's account is distorted by madness, bias, lies or limited understanding, so the reader must question it.
items.markingKey: A reliable narrator gives an account the reader can trust; an unreliable narrator's account is distorted by madness, bias, lies or limited understanding, so the reader must question it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Write the first two sentences of a Gothic story set in an abandoned school.
items.answer: Credit Gothic conventions (isolation, decay, a mystery, foreboding) and a hook. 1 mark for atmosphere, 1 for hook.
items.markingKey: Credit Gothic conventions (isolation, decay, a mystery, foreboding) and a hook. 1 mark for atmosphere, 1 for hook.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a playscript for young actors.

SCENE 2. A school hall. Night. Rain hammers on the roof. The lights flicker.
ANA: (whispering) Did you hear that?
LUCAS: It's the wind. (He doesn't look up from his phone.)
ANA: The wind doesn't knock three times.
(A knock. Three times. LUCAS slowly lowers his phone.)
LUCAS: (forcing a laugh) OK. That's... a very polite wind.
(The lights go out. Blackout.)

Analyse how the writer uses sentence structure in "That's... a very polite wind." to create tension.
items.answer: Humour / comic relief: "That's... a very polite wind." – Lucas's nervous joke releases tension briefly and reveals he is scared.
items.markingKey: Humour / comic relief: "That's... a very polite wind." – Lucas's nervous joke releases tension briefly and reveals he is scared. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a Gothic short story told by a teenage narrator.

My brother says I imagine things. He's probably right. I imagined the scratching behind the wallpaper. I imagined that the mirror in the hall shows the room as it was a hundred years ago – the gas lamps, the dark curtains, the woman in grey.
Last night I imagined she turned round.
This morning there were wet footprints on the stairs. Small ones. Bare.
My brother says I must have walked in my sleep. I didn't tell him that my feet were dry.

Explain how the writer makes something familiar seem strange or threatening.
items.answer: The ordinary mirror shows the room as it was a century ago, and a reflection turns round – the familiar household object becomes impossible and threatening.
items.markingKey: The ordinary mirror shows the room as it was a century ago, and a reflection turns round – the familiar household object becomes impossible and threatening. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Identify two clues in the mirror story that make the narrator seem unreliable and one clue that suggests she is telling the truth.
items.answer: Unreliable: "He's probably right"; repeated "I imagined". Truth: her feet were dry although there were wet footprints.
items.markingKey: Unreliable: "He's probably right"; repeated "I imagined". Truth: her feet were dry although there were wet footprints.

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: a schoolbag left on a bench at a bus stop in heavy rain; the bus's red tail-lights disappear around the corner.]

Write the opening paragraph (about 150 words) of a story inspired by this image. Hook the reader and establish the mood.
items.answer: Indicative content: establishes a frustrated and lonely mood; possible idea – a missed bus that changes a day, a forgotten bag that holds a secret, or a moment of rebellion; techniques such as pathetic fallacy, a twist, short paragraphs; a hook that raises a question.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: establishes a frustrated and lonely mood; possible idea – a missed bus that changes a day, a forgotten bag that holds a secret, or a moment of rebellion; techniques such as pathetic fallacy, a twist, short paragraphs; a hook that raises a question. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Sentence structure creates more tension than vocabulary."
items.answer: Sentence structure and vocabulary work together, but structure is often what turns frightening words into a heart-stopping moment.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rhythm controls pace and shock; fragments and white space create pauses. Arguments against: vivid, threatening words create fear; tension comes from both together. Supported judgement: Sentence structure and vocabulary work together, but structure is often what turns frightening words into a heart-stopping moment.

items.stem: "Gothic fiction is still effective for modern teenage readers." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Gothic remains effective because its psychological fear and the uncanny still unsettle readers, even if some conventions are updated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fear and mystery are universal; modern horror films and games borrow Gothic conventions. Arguments against: old-fashioned settings and language can feel distant; readers are used to faster, more explicit horror. Supported judgement: Gothic remains effective because its psychological fear and the uncanny still unsettle readers, even if some conventions are updated. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "An unreliable narrator makes a story more frightening than a reliable one."
items.answer: Unreliable narrators often heighten fear through ambiguity, but a reliable narrator can be equally frightening when we trust their account of horror.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: uncertainty about reality creates dread; the reader is trapped inside a disturbed mind. Arguments against: a trustworthy narrator can make the reader believe the horror is real; too much uncertainty can confuse. Supported judgement: Unreliable narrators often heighten fear through ambiguity, but a reliable narrator can be equally frightening when we trust their account of horror.
